name: Lusaka
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Lusaka: mining and energy counterparties, procurement risk, arbitration support and ownership research.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Lusaka, scoped from Nashville: background research on counterparties in Zambia's mining, energy and construction sectors, procurement and public-contract diligence in the national capital, and factual support for counsel in disputes before the Lusaka courts and the Lusaka International Arbitration Centre.
intro: Lusaka is Zambia's capital and its principal centre of government, finance and commerce. Lusaka District recorded about 2.2 million people at the 2022 census, up from about 1.75 million in 2010, and Lusaka Province about 3.1 million, making it one of the fastest-growing cities in southern Africa. Although Zambia's copper is mined on the Copperbelt and in North-Western Province, decisions about mining licences, power, infrastructure and finance are taken in Lusaka, where the ministries, the Bank of Zambia, the Lusaka Securities Exchange, the Zambia Development Agency and the Patents and Companies Registration Agency are based. Construction, manufacturing, trading and services make up much of the city's own economy, supported by multi-facility economic zones and industrial parks.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Lusaka because it is where Zambian deals are negotiated and where state counterparties sit. Mining and energy investors need to understand who stands behind local partners, contractors and licence holders, and whether those people have political connections. Lenders and bondholders following Zambia's debt restructuring want reliable information on borrowers and guarantors. Public procurement in roads, power and construction carries bribery and conflict-of-interest risks. Since 2024 the Lusaka International Arbitration Centre has given parties a local seat for commercial disputes, and counsel on both sides of arbitrations and High Court proceedings need documented facts on parties, assets and related companies.

matters.title: Mining and energy partner diligence
matters.text: Background research on Zambian partners, contractors and licence holders in copper, emerging minerals and power projects negotiated in Lusaka, covering ownership through PACRA and the beneficial ownership register, litigation, political exposure and adverse media, so investors understand who they are entering into business with.

matters.title: Public procurement and contractor review
matters.text: Researching the owners, directors and related companies of contractors and suppliers winning government work in roads, power and construction, to identify links to officials, shell entities, repeat failures to deliver and conflicts of interest before clients partner with them, finance them or acquire them.

matters.title: Lender and creditor asset research
matters.text: Identifying publicly documented assets, related companies and litigation of Zambian borrowers, guarantors and judgment debtors, so lenders and their counsel can assess recovery prospects and decide whether High Court enforcement or registration of an arbitral award in Lusaka is likely to be worthwhile.

matters.title: Arbitration and litigation fact support
matters.text: Supporting counsel in disputes seated at the Lusaka International Arbitration Centre or heard in the Lusaka High Court by assembling documented facts on opposing parties, corporate histories, witnesses' public records and related entities, using lawful sources and leaving evidence collection to counsel's procedures.

matters.title: Agricultural and trading counterparty checks
matters.text: Verifying grain, fertiliser, fuel and import-export traders based in Lusaka, including their shareholders, track record, disputes and connections to public bodies, to help buyers, financiers and development institutions assess fraud, diversion and reputational risk in supply and offtake contracts.

local_context.title: Lusaka High Court
local_context.text: The High Court in Lusaka sits on Independence Avenue, close to the Supreme Court and the Ministry of Justice, in a building completed in the 1960s. Its work is organised in divisions including the General List, Commercial, Family and Children's, Criminal, and Constitutional and Human Rights. Commercial disputes involving Zambian companies are frequently heard in the Commercial Division in Lusaka, and the High Court also has jurisdiction over arbitration matters, including enforcement of awards.

local_context.title: Lusaka International Arbitration Centre
local_context.text: The Lusaka International Arbitration Centre was commissioned on 5 April 2024, launched by President Hakainde Hichilema, to administer international and domestic arbitrations and other forms of dispute resolution. A 2025 baseline recorded seven cases involving 15 parties, valued from about USD 10,000 to USD 40 million, with energy the largest share. Its rules require disclosure of third-party funders, and it has partnered with Jus Mundi to publish non-confidential awards.

local_context.title: Arbitration law and reform
local_context.text: Arbitration seated in Lusaka is governed by the Arbitration Act No. 19 of 2000, based on the 1985 UNCITRAL Model Law, and set-aside applications must be brought within three months of the award. No specialist arbitration court has been designated. A draft Alternative Dispute Resolution Bill was delivered to government in February 2026 but had not been enacted as of August 2026, so procedural rules may change.

local_context.title: PACRA and national registries
local_context.text: The Patents and Companies Registration Agency, a semi-autonomous agency of the Ministry of Commerce, handles incorporation and maintains the companies and beneficial ownership registers from Lusaka. Foreign companies must lodge annual accounts. Because PACRA records depend on what filers submit and are not always current, entries are compared with litigation, procurement and media records rather than taken at face value, and gaps are reported to the client.

local_context.title: Economic zones and investment agency
local_context.text: The Zambia Development Agency, established under the ZDA Act No. 17 of 2022, promotes investment and administers incentives, and Zambia has five multi-facility economic zones and two industrial parks in operation. Companies in industrial parks may benefit from tax incentives, so diligence confirms that an investor's zone status, licences and actual operations match what it claims in applications and contracts.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Lusaka, TDSC begins by defining the decision the client faces, whether that is entering a mining partnership, financing a contractor or preparing for an arbitration, and then identifies the records that bear on it: PACRA company and beneficial ownership data, Lusaka High Court and appellate judgments, procurement notices and Zambian media. Research is conducted from Nashville. Where court file searches, site visits or interviews in Lusaka are needed, TDSC coordinates with qualified local professionals and the client's Zambian counsel. Political exposure is assessed carefully and stated with its evidence, and personal data is collected only as far as the matter requires.

faqs.q: Can you identify who really owns a Lusaka company?
faqs.a: We start with the PACRA company record and the beneficial ownership register, then test the declared owners against litigation, procurement awards, media reports and related companies. Where the registered owners appear to be nominees or the structure runs through other jurisdictions, we follow the chain as far as lawful public sources allow and state clearly where it stops.

faqs.q: How do you support an arbitration at the Lusaka International Arbitration Centre?
faqs.a: We assemble documented facts on the opposing party, including corporate history, related entities, assets and prior disputes, for counsel to evaluate. Because the centre began operating in 2024 and many awards are confidential, we also look for related High Court proceedings, such as enforcement or set-aside applications, that may be public.

faqs.q: Do you assess political exposure of Zambian partners?
faqs.a: Yes. In a capital where business and government closely interact, we look for documented links between a counterparty's owners or directors and public officials, state bodies or political parties. We report what the evidence shows and its source, distinguishing confirmed relationships from rumour, so clients can make proportionate compliance decisions.

faqs.q: Are Lusaka court records easy to search?
faqs.a: Published judgments of the Supreme Court, Court of Appeal and High Court are a useful starting point, but coverage is incomplete and many case files are only accessible at the registry. Where a file search matters, we arrange it through Zambian counsel or qualified local professionals rather than relying on online sources alone.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Lusaka?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office or staff in Lusaka or elsewhere in Zambia. Most of our work is desk-based research. Where on-the-ground steps are needed, we coordinate with qualified local professionals acting lawfully and with the client's Zambian counsel, and we do not seek restricted government records.
